bodies.Banner: Transform the supplied reference image into a finished 2000 x 300 ultra-wide advertising banner. This is a deliberate banner reconstruction, not a stretched resize and not a crop of the original composition. Preserve the source brand identity, campaign idea, language, colors, materials, photographic style, product appearance, person or IP identity, and visual tone. Recompose the design into a clear left-to-right hierarchy that works naturally in an extremely shallow 20:3 canvas. Keep the brand logo, primary headline, primary hero product or person, and primary call to action or URL fully visible, legible, undistorted, and separated from one another. Treat each connected logo, text, UI, product, device, or person group as one rigid unit when moving or scaling it. Preserve exact wording whenever readable from the reference; do not translate, paraphrase, misspell, replace, duplicate, or invent brand names, headlines, prices, URLs, labels, logos, badges, product details, faces, hands, devices, or interface content. Use secondary details only when they remain readable and do not crowd the primary hierarchy. If the source contains more information than can remain legible in a 300-pixel-high banner, prioritize the brand, main message, hero subject, and primary CTA rather than shrinking every element into unreadable clutter. Extend or regenerate only the nonsemantic background and expendable decoration needed to fill the ultra-wide canvas naturally. The background must remain visually continuous across the full width with source-matched lighting, gradients, texture, perspective, and depth. Do not create edge-pixel stretching, mirrored seams, repeated objects, empty padding, white bars, solid filler bands, frames, masks, hard crop lines, abrupt blur transitions, or visibly synthetic side extensions. Keep all meaning-bearing content comfortably inside the canvas edges. Before finalizing, visually audit that no text, logo, CTA, face, hand, product, device, or business-critical object is clipped, malformed, hidden, or touching an edge. Output one complete horizontal banner only, with no mockup, border, crop marks, alternative layout, explanatory text, or transparent checkerboard.
bodies.BannerFlash8: Transform the supplied reference image into one finished ultra-wide advertising composition on an 8:1 generation canvas. The production system will make one deterministic centered crop from the generated 8:1 image and convert that crop into a final 2000 x 300, 20:3 banner. Design the centered 20:3 region as the actual finished advertisement. The surrounding horizontal area exists only to support the deterministic crop. This is a deliberate professional banner reconstruction. It is not a stretched resize, a direct crop, a mirrored extension, or a collection of unrelated elements. PLANNING BEFORE COMPOSITION: Before drawing, silently inspect the reference image and identify every independent brand logo; product family and model name; primary headline or campaign message; secondary selling points and specifications; prices, dates, benefits, badges, platform cards, CTA, search bar, or URL; hero product, person, device, interface, and supporting objects; background, scene, lighting, texture, lines, patterns, and nonsemantic decoration; the original number of meaningful occurrences of every semantic group; and the single element that should become the strongest visual anchor. Do not output this analysis. Use it only to plan the banner. CONTENT PRIORITY: When all source information cannot remain legible in a 300-pixel-high banner, preserve content in this order: independent brand logo; core product, campaign, or marketing message; hero product or person; primary CTA, URL, price, date, or purchase information; important benefits, specifications, badges, and secondary information; expendable decoration. Never remove an independent brand logo merely because the same brand name also appears inside a headline, product, screen, package, or badge. LAYOUT SELECTION: Choose exactly one primary composition strategy based on the reference. Do not combine several incompatible templates. STRATEGY A — LARGE TITLE AND PRODUCT ARRAY: Use when the product name, model name, campaign title, or series name is the strongest message, especially when the source includes multiple product colors or views. Use one large title area. Use a product array or hero product as the opposing visual anchor. Keep secondary information between or beneath those anchors. Allow strong scale contrast. Do not make every element equally prominent. STRATEGY B — THREE VISUAL ANCHORS: Use when the source contains a brand or model, a central marketing message or CTA, and a hero person or product. Place the brand and product identity in one area, the primary marketing information in a second area, and the hero person or product in a third area. The three areas must not look like equal mechanical columns. Use scale, lighting, overlap, and negative space to establish a clear hierarchy. STRATEGY C — CENTERED CAMPAIGN: Use when an event, promotion, competition, reward, launch, or campaign message is more important than an individual product. Keep the campaign message as the central focal point. Use brand marks, products, people, or environmental elements to balance both sides. Preserve the scene and direct background lighting or perspective toward the center. Do not split the main campaign message into unrelated sections. STRATEGY D — COMMERCE MODULES: Use when the reference contains prices, platforms, bundles, benefits, purchase dates, subscription cards, or other transaction information. Keep each price, platform, benefit, or purchase-information group intact. Organize the banner into a clear horizontal sequence of product identity, features, transaction information, and product display. Treat a connected commerce card as one rigid unit. Never separate a price from its currency, platform, storage option, date, or associated benefit. Do not create additional prices, platforms, cards, or offers. STRATEGY E — HORIZONTAL STORY: Use when the source intentionally contains several products, messages, colors, features, or narrative stages. Create three to five clear horizontal story nodes. Give every node a distinct purpose. Connect the nodes through spacing, background direction, visual lines, perspective, or repeated source styling. Preserve meaningful repeated products or logos when they already serve different roles in the reference. Do not create a new repeated node that communicates nothing new. SEMANTIC COUNT AND DUPLICATION: Preserve every independent semantic group and its intended number of occurrences from the reference. Do not add a second version of a headline, benefit row, CTA, URL, price card, badge set, logo, product, person, gift, device, or interface unless multiple distinct occurrences already exist in the reference. Repeated source elements may be preserved only when they clearly serve different original functions, such as different product colors or views, separate narrative stages, a standalone brand logo and a brand name inside a product or headline, several platform or price cards, or intentional campaign repetition. Never duplicate an element merely to fill empty space. TEXT AND BRAND ACCURACY: Preserve the original language and exact readable wording. Do not translate, paraphrase, rewrite, shorten, misspell, replace, or invent brand names, product names, headlines, prices, dates, capacities, measurements, URLs, CTA labels, benefits, badges, product details, or interface content. Keep every connected text, logo, UI, price, badge, or commerce group structurally intact when moving or scaling it. VISUAL HIERARCHY: The finished banner must have exactly one strongest visual anchor, no more than two secondary visual anchors, clearly subordinate supporting information, an intentional left-to-right reading path, strong but controlled differences in scale, and enough negative space to separate unrelated information. Do not distribute all content evenly across the canvas. Do not make every object and text block the same size. The main title, campaign message, price, person, or product may be the strongest anchor depending on the source. BACKGROUND AND HORIZONTAL CONTINUITY: Preserve the source background identity, colors, lighting, texture, materials, scene, depth, perspective, and visual direction. Use the background to connect the horizontal composition. Background extension may use source-matched gradients, continuous environmental scenery, low-contrast patterns, source-derived lines or motion, lighting falloff, texture, and expendable nonsemantic decoration. Do not introduce a new visual theme unrelated to the source. Do not enlarge a secondary decoration, local background shape, gift, badge, pattern, or prop until it becomes an unintended main visual. Do not create edge-pixel stretching, mirrored scenery, repeated background objects, blurred filler strips, white bars, solid padding bands, frames, masks, abrupt seams, hard lighting transitions, or empty artificial margins. FINAL CROP SAFETY: The outermost 15 percent on both the left and right sides of the 8:1 generation canvas are crop-risk support areas. Place every meaning-bearing element fully inside the central 70 percent, from x = 15 percent through x = 85 percent, with comfortable internal padding. This applies to every independent logo, complete letter and text line, product and model name, price and number, date and URL, CTA and search bar, badge and commerce card, product and device, person, face and hand, interface, and business-critical object. The final 20:3 banner does not need empty sides. Important content may appear visually close to the final banner edges, provided it remains safely inside the central semantic region of the 8:1 generation canvas before cropping. INTENTIONAL EDGE CROSSING: Nonsemantic decoration, environmental scenery, lighting, patterns, motion lines, confetti, ribbons, particles, or similar details may enter or leave the final 20:3 frame. A product or person may also use intentional visual bleed only when its identity, face, hand, product form, and essential silhouette remain clear. Every edge crossing must look intentional and visually continuous. Do not leave an isolated sliver, a tiny unrecognizable fragment, an accidental half-shape, a broken contour, a disconnected particle, a hard crop scar, or an object that appears damaged by cropping. Preserve the direction, scale, density, spacing, contour, and visual flow of anything crossing the final frame edge. FINAL AUDIT: Before finalizing, silently inspect the centered 20:3 finished region and confirm that the selected composition strategy is clear; there is one dominant visual anchor; every independent source logo is retained; every important semantic group appears in the correct intended quantity; no new duplicate information has been created; all critical wording, numbers, dates, prices, and URLs remain accurate; no important element enters the crop-risk support areas; products, people, faces, hands, devices, and interfaces remain recognizable; the background is continuous; every edge crossing appears intentional and coherent; and no fragment, seam, stretching, mirror, filler band, or malformed content is visible. Output one complete horizontal image only. Do not output a mockup, alternative layout, border, crop mark, safe-area guide, explanatory text, transparent checkerboard, or multiple design options.
